strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: inference-time multi-preference alignment (arbitrary user-specified reward weights w and KL regularization factor λ) without additional fine-tuning is a practical and timely problem for diffusion model deployment.

Principled technical foundation: Proposition 1 derives the control-term representation of the aligned backward SDE from first principles (with a simpler proof than prior stochastic-control-based derivations, e.g., Uehara et al. 2024b), Lemma 1 provides a bound on the Jensen-gap approximation error, and Lemma 2 directly enables the linear blending algorithms.

The two resulting algorithms (DB-MPA for multi-reward blending, DB-KLA for KL-strength control) are simple, computationally efficient at inference (~2x cost of a single-model baseline, vs. 20-40x for CoDe/RGG), and DB-KLA's extrapolation regime (λ > 1) is a genuinely useful diagnostic/control knob not offered by prior fine-tuning approaches.

Reasonable baseline coverage: parameter-space interpolation (Rewarded Soup), gradient-based guidance (RGG), gradient-free guidance (CoDe), and an oracle MORL upper bound, evaluated on both train and held-out test prompts, plus extension to m=3 rewards and fine-grained weight granularity.
Good reproducibility signals: code released, pseudo-code for both algorithms, prompt lists, and detailed hyperparameter/training configurations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core mechanism is conceptually simple (averaging the predicted drifts/denoising outputs of independently fine-tuned models), and the main theoretical result (Proposition 1) closely mirrors Uehara et al. [2024b], which the authors acknowledge. The genuinely new theory (Lemma 1) is a loose, assumption-heavy bound whose terms (Lt,1, Lt,2, Lt,3) are never measured empirically, so the approximation quality of the blending is unquantified in practice.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only Stable Diffusion v1.5, only 25 training prompts (DrawBench 'color' category) and 25 GPT-4-generated color-object prompts. This synthetic, color-dominated prompt distribution limits claims of general applicability. No human evaluation, no FID/precision-recall/diversity metrics—results are judged solely by the same reward models used for fine-tuning, raising circularity/reward-hacking concerns the paper does not examine.

Reported gaps to the oracle are nontrivial (e.g., at w=0.8, DB-MPA r1 = 0.83 vs. MORL 0.90; r2 = 0.03 vs. -0.14), yet the text repeatedly claims performance 'close to' the oracle; the degree of Pareto-front optimality should be stated more carefully. No statistical variance or significance testing is reported despite reward-model noise.

Approximation validity for λ > 1 (extrapolation, not interpolation) in DB-KLA is not theoretically supported—the error terms in Eq. (10) scale with λ and could blow up—and the failure mode for small α is only qualitatively discussed (via Lemma 1) rather than empirically characterized.

The paper does not compare against the natural alternative of jointly fine-tuning on a weighted reward combination (DRaFT-style) or against a single model fine-tuned on the mixture, which would clarify when inference-time blending is preferable to a modest extra fine-tune. Memory cost of holding m full U-Nets is acknowledged but unaddressed.

Multiple presentation errors undermine polish: Eq. (11) in the proof of Proposition 1 has the same term on both sides (apparently ∇ log p_t^tar should be ∇ log p_t^pre); the Lemma 2 proof ends with a dangling '+'; VILA is misattributed to Kirstain et al. in Section 5.1 (it is Ke et al.); the abstract's code link is incomplete.

strengths: The problem of inference-time multi-preference alignment (arbitrary reward weights and KL regularization strength without re-fine-tuning) is well-motivated and practically relevant for deployment scenarios.

The paper provides a clean theoretical framing: Proposition 1 gives a first-principles decomposition of the fine-tuned backward SDE drift into the pre-trained drift plus a control term, and Lemma 2 shows how drifts compose under linear reward combinations, directly justifying the algorithms.

Experiments include relevant baselines (Rewarded Soup, CoDe, reward gradient guidance) and a MORL oracle upper bound; DB-MPA approaches oracle performance at modest inference overhead (2x the base model) and much lower cost than CoDe/RGG.
The paper is clearly written, with pseudo-code, hyperparameters, prompt lists, and a code release promise, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core theory: the authors themselves acknowledge that Proposition 1 is essentially the control-as-inference result of Uehara et al. [2024b] re-derived; the remaining contribution is a heuristic Jensen-gap approximation leading to what is effectively score/drift averaging, which is an intuitive and fairly straightforward operation.

The approximation error bound (Lemma 1) has questionable practical content: terms like L_{t,3} involve a supremum over unregularized gradients of a conditional density and rely on unverifiable shift-family assumptions; the bound is never empirically validated or connected to observed approximation error.

Narrow evaluation scope: only Stable Diffusion v1.5, only 25 training and 25 GPT-4-generated test prompts restricted to color-object descriptions, and main results limited to m=2 rewards; this is far from demonstrating the claimed 'extensive experiments' or generalization to diverse prompts, styles, or reward families.

Evaluation reward models are the same as the fine-tuning rewards (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore), raising self-evaluation/reward-gaming concerns; there is no human evaluation, no held-out reward metric, and no statistical significance or variance reporting across seeds.

The DB-KLA result is largely an interpolation between pre-trained and fine-tuned drifts, which resembles existing logit/parameter interpolation (e.g., DeRa, RS); the paper overstates the contrast, and the λ > 1 regime lacks a rigorous account of when it degrades.

Missing comparisons and baselines: no comparison to weighted-reward joint fine-tuning (DRaFT-style) as a cheap alternative, no ablation on the number of fine-tuned models vs. coverage (exponential growth concern is acknowledged but not studied), and no analysis of failure modes at extreme w or small α despite the theory predicting them.

Some presentations are imprecise: e.g., the reward model attributions (VILA vs. PickScore description inconsistencies), the bound in Eq. (12)-(14) details, and figures with low readability (Pareto-front labels) reduce polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: inference-time multi-preference alignment over linear reward combinations and KL regularization strengths, addressing a genuine practical limitation of fixed-reward RL fine-tuning.

Principled theoretical foundation: Proposition 1 derives the controlled backward SDE from first principles, Lemma 1 provides an explicit upper bound on the Jensen-gap approximation error, and Lemma 2 connects the blended drift to the desired target drift. The paper honestly contrasts its derivation with Uehara et al. (2024b) and discusses when the approximation may fail (small alpha).

The resulting algorithms (DB-MPA, DB-KLA) are simple, practical, and computationally efficient at inference time (~2x the cost of a single model), in contrast to expensive multi-particle guidance methods like CoDe (185s/img) and RGG (122s/img).

Comprehensive baselines including parameter-space interpolation (Rewarded Soup), gradient-based guidance (RGG), gradient-free search (CoDe), and an oracle MORL upper bound; DB-MPA's Pareto front is close to the oracle and clearly dominates the other baselines.

Both quantitative (reward evaluations on held-out test prompts, m=2 and m=3 reward settings, inference-time table) and qualitative evidence (smooth control over w and lambda, finer-grained w sweeps), plus reproducibility details (prompts, hyperparameters, hardware) and code release.

The DB-KLA result (controlling effective KL weight via blending fine-tuned and pretrained models, including lambda > 1 extrapolation) is a novel and useful capability for diffusion models with no direct LLM analogue.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: only SDv1.5 (an older base model), 25 training prompts and 25 test prompts, all simple color-object compositions. Generalization to complex prompts, higher-resolution models (SDXL), and other fine-tuning algorithms (beyond DPOK) is not demonstrated.

Evaluation uses the same reward models (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore) that were optimized during fine-tuning, so measured gains could partly reflect reward overoptimization; no held-out/orthogonal metrics or human evaluation is provided to validate perceptual quality.

The main technical result (Proposition 1) is closely related to Uehara et al. (2024b), and Lemma 1 relies on assumptions (bounded sub-Gaussian rewards, exponential tail decay) whose tightness in practice is not empirically validated; the decomposition-based proof of Lemma 3 could be scrutinized further.

Practical costs are understated: the method requires storing and running m separately fine-tuned models, doubling memory and inference time for m=2 (and scaling linearly in m); the discussion of this limitation is brief and no mitigation (e.g., LoRA-based blending or distillation experiments) is attempted.

Theory assumes linear scalarization of rewards and that each fine-tuned model is well-aligned with its basis reward; behavior under conflicting rewards, non-convex preference regions, or poorly converged fine-tuning is not analyzed.

Presentation issues: several typos and minor errors (e.g., 'Multi-Prefence', 'SVv1.5', VILA mis-cited as Kirstain et al. on page 8, a likely typo in Eq. (11) where p^tar appears on both sides, duplicate B.3 section numbering), which slightly reduce polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: inference-time multi-preference alignment (arbitrary reward weights w and KL rescaling λ without re-fine-tuning) addresses a real practical limitation of RL fine-tuning for diffusion models.

Solid theoretical scaffolding: Proposition 1 derives the drift of the aligned model as the pre-trained drift plus a control term via a simple first-principles proof; Lemma 1 provides an interpretable upper bound on the Jensen-gap approximation error; Lemma 2 gives the key linear-blending result; Proposition 2 gives a rigorous SDE justification for the LoRA-sampling variant achieving identical marginals.

Extensive and well-designed evaluation: comparisons against relevant and diverse baselines (Rewarded Soup, CoDe, RGG, and an explicit MORL oracle upper bound), two prompt benchmarks (Short-DrawBench and GenEval with held-out test sets), scaling to 2–4 rewards, adversarial conflicting rewards (JPEG compressibility), an SDXL extension, and inference-time measurements showing DB-MPA-LS removes the m× overhead.

The lightweight DB-MPA-LS variant is practically valuable, achieving near-DB-MPA performance at essentially Stable Diffusion inference cost, backed by theory (Proposition 2) rather than just heuristics.
Code availability, pseudo-code, detailed hyperparameters, and transparent discussion of when the approximation may fail (small α) improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Core theory is partially derivative: Proposition 1 closely mirrors the control-term result in Uehara et al. (2024b), which the authors acknowledge; the genuinely new theoretical content (Jensen-gap bound, Lemma 2, Proposition 2) is useful but incremental.

Key approximations are dropped in practice without verification: the error terms ∆ in Lemma 2 are discarded in DB-MPA/DB-KLA, and the bound in Lemma 1 rests on assumptions (bounded/sub-Gaussian rewards, near-shift-family conditionals) that are assumed rather than empirically validated; no experiment quantifies the actual approximation error of drift blending versus the exact aligned drift.

The entire framework implicitly assumes each RL fine-tuned model converges to the closed-form KL-regularized optimum (eq. 6); deviations of practical RL (DPOK/PPO) from this optimum are not characterized, yet blending quality depends on it.

Training/evaluation scale is narrow: RL fine-tuning uses only 25 color prompts (Short-DrawBench) and 550 GenEval prompts; the SDXL experiment is a single prompt. Generalization claims rest largely on GPT-4-generated test prompts, which are semantically close to training prompts.

Evaluation relies on the same reward models used for training (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore), raising reward-overfitting concerns; there is no human evaluation or FID/diversity metric to check whether alignment degrades sample quality, despite the paper's motivation emphasizing diversity preservation.

Minor but noticeable citation/consistency errors (e.g., VILA attributed to Kirstain et al. 2023, GenEval attributed to the Pick-a-pic paper), and the claim that DB-MPA 'consistently outperforms' baselines is slightly overstated given cases where CoDe wins on r1 (e.g., w=0.8 in Table 1).

Restriction to linear scalarization over the simplex limits the preference space; the paper does not discuss or test non-linear preference aggregation, and DB-MPA-LS inherits Bernoulli/categorical sampling whose discrete-time behavior (shared noise across steps) is argued only in the continuous-time idealization.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: inference-time multi-preference (multi-reward and multi-KL) alignment of diffusion models without retraining for each preference configuration.

The theoretical development is reasonably complete: Proposition 1 gives a control-term decomposition of the aligned reverse SDE, Lemma 1/3 provides a Jensen-gap-based error bound for the approximation, and Proposition 2 justifies the LoRA-sampling variant (DB-MPA-LS) via an SDE marginal-equivalence argument.
Three concrete algorithms are proposed, including a computationally efficient variant (DB-MPA-LS) that removes the m× inference overhead, which is a practical contribution.

The experimental evaluation is broad: multiple reward models, two prompt benchmarks, a MORL oracle upper bound, an adversarial/conflicting-reward setting, scaling from 2 to 4 rewards, and an SDXL extension, with reasonable baselines (Rewarded Soup, CoDe, RGG).
Code is stated to be available, and implementation details (hyperparameters, hardware, prompt generation) are given in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core idea: linearly combining reverse-process drifts/scores of individually fine-tuned models is a natural and fairly incremental extension. Proposition 1 substantially overlaps with Uehara et al. (2024b) (acknowledged by the authors), and the algorithmic contribution is close to Rewarded Soup (parameter averaging) and LLM decoding-time realignment methods; the delta over these works is modest.

The gap between theory and practice is not validated empirically. The algorithms drop the approximation error terms Δ(r,α) in Lemma 2, and the error bound in Lemma 1/3 involves quantities (Lt,1, Lt,2, Lt,3) that are never measured or verified in experiments; in particular, Lt,3 grows as α decreases, so the bound may be vacuous for small KL weights, yet no empirical check of approximation quality is provided. The assumption that DPOK fine-tuning converges to the closed-form solution of eq. (3) is stated but never validated.

Evaluation has a circularity problem: all quantitative results are measured with the same reward models (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore) that were used for fine-tuning, so 'superior reward scores' could partly reflect reward overoptimization, which the paper's own motivation identifies as a failure mode. No human evaluation, no ground-truth fidelity/diversity metrics (e.g., FID), and no evaluation on held-out reward models are reported.

The evaluation domain is narrow: Short-DrawBench training uses only 25 color-category prompts, and the 1,000-prompt test set is generated by GPT-4 to be 'semantically similar' to the training prompts. GenEval fine-tuning likewise uses 550 prompts with test prompts from the same generation toolkit. Generalization claims rest on a narrow color/object-composition distribution; the SDXL experiment is a single prompt.

Some theoretical statements are weakened by sloppiness: the proof of Proposition 1 contains an evident typo (eq. 11 has ∇ log p^tar_t on both sides; the left side should be p^pre_t), typos throughout ('Inferrence', 'Prefence', 'Winner process'), and the claimed Pareto-optimality is asserted qualitatively but never formally established or measured against the oracle beyond visual inspection of Pareto plots.

DB-KLA's extrapolation regime (λ > 1) and the λ=0 identification of SDv1.5 with 'infinite regularization weight' are heuristic; there is no theoretical or empirical calibration of how effective KL weight α/λ relates to the blending coefficient λ outside the approximation regime.

Missing comparisons with other multi-objective training-free guidance baselines (e.g., multi-objective guidance of Han et al., 2023), and the RGG baseline was modified (per-reward gradient normalization) without ablation showing this does not disadvantage it.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: inference-time multi-preference alignment for diffusion models with user-specified reward weights and KL regularization is practically relevant and, unlike parameter merging (Rewarded Soup), grounded in the drift of the backward SDE.

Coherent theoretical treatment: Proposition 1 gives a first-principles derivation of the reward-dependent control term, Lemma 1/3 provides an explicit upper bound on the Jensen-gap approximation error with interpretable terms, and Lemma 2 yields the linear drift blending used by DB-MPA/DB-KLA. Proposition 2 is a clean SDE argument justifying the zero-overhead LoRA-sampling variant.

Extensive and reasonably fair empirical evaluation: two reward settings plus 3- and 4-reward extensions, a conflicting/adversarial reward case (JPEG vs. aesthetics), GenEval generalization tests, an SDXL scaling experiment, multiple relevant baselines (RS, CoDe, RGG, and MORL as an oracle), and inference-time measurements. DB-MPA-LS achieving near-MORL Pareto performance at SD-speed is a convincing headline result.

Honest positioning: prior art (Uehara et al. for the control result, Rewarded Soup as the closest baseline, LLM decoding-time realignment) is clearly acknowledged, and the MORL oracle is used to contextualize gains rather than overclaim.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the control-term result is acknowledged to be similar to Uehara et al. (2024b), the Jensen-gap interchange is standard in diffusion guidance (DPS, Rout et al.), and the final algorithms reduce to weighting the drifts of existing fine-tuned models. The main genuinely new technical piece is the sampling proposition and the error decomposition.

The central approximation f^(r(w),α) ≈ Σ w_i f^(ri,α) drops the Jensen-gap error terms, whose magnitude is never measured empirically. Moreover, each f^(ri,α) is itself an RL-learned approximation of the ideal drift under eq. (4), a second error source not accounted for in the theory; the closeness to MORL remains purely empirical.

Evaluation is confined to narrow, LLM-generated color-object prompt sets (25 Short-DrawBench prompts, GPT-4 test prompts explicitly generated to be 'semantically similar to the training set', GenEval), raising train/test distribution overlap concerns; no evaluation on diverse open-ended benchmarks, and no human evaluation, FID, or diversity metrics despite claims that KL regularization preserves sample quality/diversity.
Rewards used for evaluation (ImageReward, VILA, PickScore) are the same as those used for fine-tuning, so improvements partly measure reward-model overfitting rather than genuine generation quality.

Multiple technical and writing defects: eq. (11) contains an obvious typo (∇ log p_t^tar appearing on both sides; should be p_t^pre); the Prop. 1 proof uses a variance-exploding forward process inconsistent with the VP formulation introduced earlier; Proposition 2 requires Y_t independent of the state process, whose validity under Euler-Maruyama discretization is not verified; typos ('Multi-Prefence', 'INFERRENCE', 'SVv1.5', 'Winner process'), mislabeled figure references (fig. 3(c) vs. 6(a)), and a garbled Lemma 1 statement in the main text.

No statistical uncertainty (confidence intervals/seeds) reported for the main quantitative tables, and several figure captions claim trends (e.g., smooth control) that are supported only qualitatively.

Missing comparisons to other multi-reward diffusion alignment methods discussed in related work (Parrot, Calibrated multi-preference optimization), and the storage/memory cost of maintaining m fine-tuned models (or LoRA adapters) at deployment is not discussed.
